Introduction

This chapter provides criteria for evaluating perma-nent impairment of the digestive system, consisting of the alimentary canal, liver, biliary tract, and pan-creas. The criteria for assigning permanent impair-ment ratings of digestive system disease include clinically established or objectively determined deviations from normal in the transport and assimi-lation of ingested food, nutrition, metabolism, waste product excretion, and the effect of these problems on individuals’ performance of Activities of Daily Living (ADLs).

The chapter has been extensively revised from the Fifth Edition with regard to the impairment percent-ages assigned to each class and the overall use of the system for rating impairment as outlined in Chapter

1. As with other chapters, these changes have been adopted both to increase interrater reliability with regard to the assessment of gastrointestinal (GI) tract impairment and to allow for ratings that are com-parable to those assigned for dysfunction of other organ systems. In particular, this applies to the fol-lowing: (1) Impairments of similar gravity, which have similar impact on the ability to perform ADLs for the small and large intestine, have been given

the same impairment ratings for comparable classes. (2) Ratings of impairment from hepatic and other diseases have been revised downward due to the ten-dency, in prior editions of the Guides, for the rating to encompass both organ-system specific pathology and the affect it has on other organ systems; the rater is now encouraged to rate secondary disease processes separately and combine them with the rating for the primary gastroenterological disease. (3) Home parenteral nutrition programs have reha-bilitated some and improved the daily lives of many individuals with intestinal failure resulting from a variety of causes, but compliance with the treatment regimens does have an impact on ADLs; this is now recognized by allowing for the addition of percent-age points for “Burden of Treatment Compliance” (See Appendix B) to the GI tract impairment rating. (4) The effect of a given gastroenterological condi-tion on the ability to function is incorporated into the ratings and is also reflected by the BOTC; there is no separate “Functional Evaluation” by questionnaire in this chapter.

6.1 Principles of Assessment

Before using the information in this chapter, the Guides user should become familiar with Chapters 1 and 2 and the Glossary. Chapters 1 and 2 discuss the Guides’ purpose, applications, and methods for performing and reporting impairment evaluations. The Glossary provides definitions of common terms used by many specialties in impairment evaluation. This information should be available to determine impairment.

6.1a Interpretation of Symptoms and Signs

Some upper digestive tract symptoms limit the abil-ity to perform daily activities. As this information is subjective and subject to misinterpretation, it does not serve as the key factor for assigning impairment ratings. Rather, the examiner should obtain objec-tive data about the injury or disorder, usually from a review of pertinent medical records, and integrate those findings with the subjective data to estimate the degree of permanent impairment.

Esophageal impairment symptoms and signs include dysphagia, pyrosis or heartburn, retrosternal pain, regurgitation, bleeding, and weight loss. Note that occasional minor dyspepsia, gas, and belching are within the experience of all individuals.

Stomach and duodenum impairment symptoms and signs include nausea, vomiting, pain, bleeding, obstruction, diarrhea, weight loss, and certain types of malabsorption. Some impairments may produce nutritional deficiencies that lead to hematologic and neurologic manifestations, which would be rated separately and combined with digestive system impairments.

Small-intestine impairment symptoms and signs include abdominal pain, diarrhea, steatorrhea, bleed-ing, obstruction, and weight loss, which often are associated with general debility and other extraintes-tinal manifestations.

Pancreatic function impairment symptoms and signs include, but are not limited to, pain, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, steatorrhea, weight loss, muscle wasting, jaundice, diabetes mellitus, and debility. Impairment due to endocrine disturbance related to the pancreas is considered in the Guides chapter on the endocrine system (Chapter 10).

Colon, rectum, and anus impairment symptoms and signs include abdominal, pelvic, or perineal pain; dis-ordered bowel action; tenesmus; fecal incontinence; bleeding; suppuration; and the appearance of hemor-rhoids, fissures, and fistulas. Systemic manifestations may include fever, weight loss, debility, and anemia.

Hepatobiliary impairment symptoms and signs include pain, nausea, vomiting, anorexia, loss of strength and stamina, reduced resistance to infec-tion, altered immune response, jaundice, and pruri-tus. Advanced liver disease complications include edema and generalized ascites, portal hypertension leading to esophageal varices and hemorrhage, and metabolic disturbances leading to hepatic encepha-lopathy and renal failure.

Abdominal wall impairment symptoms and signs include typically intermittent discomfort or pain at or near the herniation site, often associated with a visible, palpable protrusion or swelling at the hernia-tion site, appearing and disappearing with postural changes or abdominal pressure. More acute and intense pain can be seen due to complications, espe-cially incarceration and strangulation of contained bowel or omentum.

Incisional hernias may be unsightly and annoying; other symptoms, if any, tend to be related to the incisional hernia size. Inguinal and femoral hernias typically are painful and entail a greater risk of incarceration or strangulation. Most abdominal wall hernias are amenable to surgical correction.

Signs and symptoms can be categorized by fre-quency, severity, and level of functional loss. Never or occasional signs or symptoms, when present up to 33% of the time, do not generally warrant an impair-ment rating (unless the ensuing disruption in ADLs is significant). Frequent signs or symptoms are present between 34% and 66% of the time, and continuous signs and symptoms are present 67% of the time and above (with it understood that this level of precision is impossible to achieve clinically). When present and in general, minimal level of signs or symptoms interfere with ADLs 1 to 10% of the time, mild signs or symptoms interfere with ADLs 11 to 25% of the time; moderate signs and symptoms affect ADLS 26 to 50% of the time and can have an impact on work and recreational activities. Severe signs or symptoms interfere with ADLs up to 51% to 75% of the time to the point of requiring modification of many routine ADLs (personal, work-related, and recreational). Extreme functional loss occurs when symptoms and signs cannot be controlled by medication and inter-fere with ADLs up to 100% of the time.

6.1b Description of Clinical Studies

Objective procedures useful in establishing esopha-geal impairment include, but are not limited to: (1) imaging procedures, such as fluoroscopy and radiog-raphy, employing contrast media; ultrasonography; and computed tomography (CT); (2) peroral and cap-sule endoscopy, including cytologic study or biopsy; and (3) functional tests, such as manometry, imped-ance, or intraesophageal pH measurement.

Objective procedures useful in establishing stomach and duodenum impairment include, but are not lim-ited to: (1) imaging techniques, such as fluoroscopy and roentgenography, with contrast media; scin-tigraphy; ultrasonography; and CT; (2) peroral and capsule endoscopy, with biopsy and cytologic study; (3) gastric secretory tests; (4) malabsorption tests; (5) stool examination; and (6) urea breath test for Helicobacter pylori.

Objective procedures useful in establishing impair-ment of the small intestine include, but are not limited to: (1) fluoroscopy and roentgenography employing contrast media; (2) peroral and capsule endoscopy and mucosal biopsy; and (3) intestinal malabsorption testing measures such as fecal fat content and urinary D-xylose excretion tests, breath tests, and Schilling test.

Objective procedures useful in establishing impair-ment of pancreatic function include, but are not lim-ited to: (1) ultrasonography; (2) radiography, including

plain or scout films of the abdomen, ultrasonogra-phy, CT, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and endoscopic pancreatography; (3) guided, fine-needle aspiration; (4) determination of plasma glucose level and glucose tolerance; (5) assay of pancreatic enzyme activity in blood, urine, and feces; (6) sweat electro-lyte test; (7) peroral endoscopy of the pancreatic and biliary tract, with biopsy and cytologic study; and (8) procedures such as the secretin test.

Objective procedures useful in establishing colon, rectum, and anus impairment include, but are not limited to: (1) digital and endoscopic examination, including anoscopy, proctoscopy, sigmoidoscopy, and colonoscopy; (2) biopsy and cytology; (3) fecal microscopy and culture; (4), rectal and colon manometry; and (5) fluoroscopy and roentgenogra-phy employing contrast media.

Objective procedures useful in establishing hepato-biliary impairment include, but are not limited to: (1) ultrasonography; (2) contrast radiography, such as percutaneous and endoscopic cholangiography; (3) CT and MRI or spiral CT; (4) nucleotide scin-tigraphy; (5) angiography; (6) liver biopsy and fine-needle aspiration; and (7) laboratory tests to assess the bile ducts and various liver functions.

Objective procedures useful in establishing impair-ment by hernias include, but are not limited to: (1) abdominal wall physical examination; and (2) imaging by roentgenography or CT scan with or without contrast media.

In general, an objective procedure is described as minimally abnormal if there is an anatomic abnor-mality that leads to no more than a 10% degree of functional organ impairment and is generally asymp-tomatic. A mild abnormality does not (or would not be expected to) lead to more than a 10% to 25% degree of functional organ impairment. A moderate abnormality would result in a 26% to 50% loss of function (if untreated), a severe abnormality would be one that is accompanied by a 51% to 75% func-tional loss (if untreated); and an extreme abnormality is one that leads to a greater than 75% loss of organ function (if untreated).

6.1d Impairment Determination

Impairment classes, as listed in Tables 6-3 through 6-10, are organ and system specific. The impairment classes and percentage ratings reflect anatomic, physi-ological, and functional abnormalities at the organ and system level and the impact of GI tract disease on ability to perform ADLs. This includes the degree to

which special dietary modifications and restrictions are required to control symptoms and signs of disease and any functional limitations that are caused by either the impairment itself or required treatment. There are some GI tract conditions in which well-recognized symptoms occur without significant anatomic or physi-ologic abnormality, but with symptoms (primarily pain) that can be either partially or completely con-trolled by simple medication. Examples would include esophageal reflux, irritable bowel syndrome, “spastic colon,” chronic constipation, or chronic abdominal pain without known origin. If the examining physician believes that conditions like these, that are otherwise not ratable by the sections and tables in this chapter, are significantly disruptive of ADLs, the physician may choose to rate these up to a 3% whole person impairment.

The definitions provided previously of “infrequent,” “occasional,” “frequent,” “constant,” “minimal,” “mild,” “moderate,” “severe,” and “extreme” as they relate to symptoms and signs are often incorporated in tables used for the determination of impairment, as are the terms “minimal,” “mild,” “moderate,” “severe,” and “extreme” as they relate to organ func-tion. The concept of BOTC is applied to this chapter according to the BOTC found in the Appendix. Due to the systemic ramifications of corticosteroid use, an additional 3% impairment can be assigned when these medications are used on a daily basis to control disease; however, the evaluator is required to provide the basis for this determination. A GI system impair-ment evaluation whose results fall in the normal range reflects an individual who performs all ADLs with only normal, occasional GI tract symptoms; no limitation of activities; no dietary modifications that interfere significantly with ADLs; and no required medication, with adequate reserve capacity that allows the body to obtain the required nutrition and maintain normal weight.

For the purposes of impairment ratings, the upper digestive tract has been defined to include the esoph-agus, stomach and duodenum, small intestine, and pancreas. Impairment criteria and classes have been combined for the colon and rectum; anal; liver and biliary impairments; and hernia impairments.

Methodology for Determining the Grade in an Impairment Class

This chapter employs impairment grids to use in determining the appropriate impairment class (class) and severity grade (grade) within a class for the condition or conditions being rated at Maximum Medical Improvement (MMI). As was stated in chapter 1, the decision regarding which factor is the primary determinant of impairment (key factor) will be clearly stated in each organ system impairment

grid. The examiner will use this key factor to deter-mine the appropriate class with the middle grade (integer) in that class as the initial (default) rating (refer to Table 6-3).

The examiner will then use non-key factors to assign grades for factors other than that considered “key,” with it being impossible to move upward or down-ward between classes based on these non-key factors. The number of potential grades for each impairment class varies based on the number of relevant factors. When there are 2 non-key factors, there are generally 5 impairment grades per class; the presence of only one relevant factor other than the key factor reduces the number of possible grades to 3 per class.

If the examiner determines that the other factors affecting the rating are in the same class that had been used for the key factor rating, the final rating will generally stay in the middle of that class. On the other hand, if the classes chosen are higher or lower than that used for the baseline impairment rat-ing, the level will be moved to the right or to the left (to a higher or lower value) to reflect the numerical discrepancy. For example, if the key factor places the initial rating in class 3, grade C and there are 2 non-key factors (leading to a total of 5 possible grades) that are in class 1 and class 4, respectively, the first factor would move the grade down 2 levels to grade A and the second would move it back up 1 level to grade B. However, if both non-key factors were class 1, the rating could not go any lower than class 3, grade A, the lowest value for the class. An exception to this rule may occur when the key factor is in the highest impairment class for the disorder, as non-key factors falling in the same class can be used to adjust the impairment rating upward to the highest grade within the class rather than keep it at the middle level. Specific tables will indicate if a rating schema other than this is used.

6.2 Upper Digestive Tract (Esophagus, Stomach and Duodenum, Small Intestine, and Pancreas)

6.2a Criteria for Rating Permanent Impairment due to Upper Digestive Tract Disease

Criteria for evaluating impairments related to upper digestive tract disease are given in Table 6-4. The history is the key factor that determines the impair-ment class. The medical records will usually permit the physician to choose the correct impairment class.

CLASS 0 0% Impairment of the Whole Person

EXAMPLE 6-1: UPPER DIGESTIVE TRACT DISEASE

Subject: 44-year-old man.

History: Warehouse stockman; transient difficulty swallowing; first occurrence 9 months ago in asso-ciation with doing a great deal of bending and heavy lifting after eating a lunch that included broiled lobster. Formerly drank large amounts of caffeinated beverages on a daily basis. Has now ceased doing so.

Current Symptoms: Infrequent symptoms of esoph-ageal disease after meals containing large amounts of protein.

Physical Exam: Within normal limits. Weight: 68.1 kg (150 lb); height: 1.78 m (5 ft 10 in); within desir-able limits. Healthy appearance; vital signs normal.

Clinical Studies: Chest roentgenogram, electrocar-diogram (ECG): normal. Barium swallow: small, sliding hiatal hernia. Endoscopy: no mucosal defect.

Diagnosis: Hiatal hernia, uncomplicated.

Impairment Rating: Class 0, 0% impairment of the whole person. Despite anatomic abnormalities, which are not work-related, history is the key factor,

and the relative absence of symptoms does not war-rant more than a class 0 rating.

Comment: The original hiatal hernia and motility disorder do not require treatment, and neither inter-feres with normal nutrition nor impairs ability to perform usual daily activities.1

EXAMPLE 6-2: STOMACH OR DUODENUM DISEASE OR INJURY

Subject: 28-year-old man.

History: 5 years’ epigastric pain and burning. Use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) for a work-related back injury caused his GI tract symp-toms to increase and was associated with minimal weight loss, but symptoms are now resolved.

Current Symptoms: Denied nausea, vomiting, hematemesis, or melena. Painful episodes had lasted up to 2 weeks, woke patient at night, and required antacids, food, and over-the-counter (OTC) H2 blockers for relief. Increased symptoms persisted despite discontinuation of NSAIDs.

Physical Exam: Height: 1.8 m (5 ft 11 in); weight: 72.6 kg (160 lb).

Clinical Studies: Barium meal: deformed duode-nal bulb. No gastric retention or pyloric stenosis. Peroral endoscopy: 1-cm duodenum ulcer-crater; considerable surrounding deformity. Antral biopsies were positive for H pylori; full-course triple-therapy (omeprazole, clarithromycin, and metronidazole) relieved symptoms. Complete healing was found at follow-up endoscopy 8 weeks later. Repeated antral biopsies: no H pylori.

Diagnosis: Resolved peptic duodenal ulcer disease associated with H pylori infection. Exacerbation of symptoms by NSAIDs—now resolved.

Impairment Rating: Class 0, 0%. He is now in remission, and test results are normal. History results in a class 0 rating.

Comment: H pylori can be found in 95% to 100% of patients with duodenal ulcer and 70% to 80% of patients with peptic stomach ulcers. Successful eradication of infection induces a long remission.2 Although NSAID use led to definitive endoscopic evaluation of his symptoms, they were not the pri-mary cause of his pathology. Had his endoscopic findings been solely consistent with NSAID-related gastritis, resolution of pathology after discontinua-tion of the medications would have still resulted in no residual impairment.

EXAMPLE 6-3: SMALL INTESTINE DISEASE

Subject: 35-year-old man.

History: Police officer stabbed in the abdomen by a knife during apprehension of a felon. On the day

of injury he had surgical closure of several holes in the small intestine, but no intestine needed to be resected. His injury was complicated by a sub-phrenic abscess that was drained percutaneously. Six months after injury he was readmitted to the hospital because of an obstruction of the small bowel that resolved without another operation. He has had occasional recurrent episodes of abdominal pain

that were identical to the bowel obstruction pain, but which resolved in a few hours, and these other epi-sodes did not require hospitalization or surgery. He uses opioids only for the most severe of his abdomi-nal pain episodes. On average he uses 5 to 10 doses of an oral opioid each year.

Current Symptoms: Has been asymptomatic for 30 days. Performs all ADLs without difficulty.

Physical Exam: Height 178 cm (5 ft 10 in). Weight: 70.3 kg (155 lb) on unrestricted diet; usual pre-illness weight: 72.6 kg (160 lb).

Clinical Studies: Flat and upright abdominal radio-graphs and an abdominal CT scan were consistent with mechanical small-bowel obstruction during his readmission.

Diagnosis: Partial, small-bowel obstruction sec-ondary to intra-abdominal adhesions from prior peritonitis.

Impairment Rating: Class 1. The table for deter-mining the appropriate class for intestinal disorders indicates that having had 1 documented episode of bowel obstruction places this police officer in class

1. He has not had the resection of any small bowel, he has not had surgery for bowel obstruction, and he has had only 1 admission for bowel obstruction, so classes 2 to 4 are not appropriate. Objective findings are class 1.

His weight is normal for his medium frame size, which can be a class 1 finding. He does use opioids, so his medication use is class 1. Thus, by the table used to determine the appropriate grade, he gets the middle integer or default rating of 5% whole person impairment.

EXAMPLE 6-4: PANCREATIC DISEASE

Subject: 40-year-old woman.

History: Bartender; episodic epigastric pain asso-ciated with elevated serum amylase activity, 2 to 3 episodes per year for 3 years. Cholecystectomy for gallstone removal 2 years ago. Reduced-energy (reduced-calorie) diet corrected exogenous obe-sity; weight did not fall below desirable level. Mild dietary restrictions.

Current Symptoms: Pain attacks, especially after large meals or immoderate alcoholic beverage consumption.

Physical Exam: Normal.

Clinical Studies: Mild elevation of amylase.

Diagnosis: Recurrent acute pancreatitis.

Impairment Rating: Class 1, 5% impairment of the whole person assigned based on intermittent symptoms and functional (based on elevated amylase level) abnormality but no weight loss.

CLASS 2 12% to 20% Impairment of the Whole Person

EXAMPLE 6-5: UPPER DIGESTIVE TRACT DISEASE

Subject: 59-year-old woman.

History: 5 years’ almost daily retrosternal pain associated with difficulty swallowing.

Current Symptoms: Symptoms less severe when diet limited to soft foods; symptoms aggravated when upset, particularly when worried. Patient has used OTC histamine-2 blockers as needed and pre-scription proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) once daily.

Physical Exam: Height: 1.7 m (5 ft 7 in), medium frame; weight: 53.6 kg (118 lb), within 10% of usual weight of 58 kg (128 lb). Blood pressure: 145/90 mm Hg. Appears older than stated age.

Clinical Studies: Chest roentgenogram, ECG: nor-mal; uncoordinated contractions in lower esophagus resulting in “corkscrew” configuration, indicative of diffuse spasm. Esophageal manometry: prolonged high amplitude, irregular synchronous contrac-tions with water swallowing, consistent with diffuse spasm. Ambulatory esophageal pH study: percentage of time that esophageal pH is less than 4 is within normal limits. Endoscopy: no mucosal defect.

Diagnosis: Diffuse spasm of the esophagus.

Impairment Rating: 16% impairment of the whole person. Symptoms, anatomic/functional abnormali-ties, and class 2 weight loss warrant the default 16% rating.

Comment: Persistent symptoms obligated woman to restrict diet. Weight loss did not exceed 10% of desirable level. Daily activities only slightly limited. Symptomatic management with agents such as nife-dipine and diltiazem hydrochloride may be helpful and sufficient; if not, surgical myotomy is reported to be beneficial in 70% to 80% of cases.3

EXAMPLE 6-6: GASTROESOPHAGEAL REFLUX DISEASE

Subject: 43-year-old man.

History: Burning retrosternal chest distress increas-ing in severity and frequency over the last 18 months. Occurred after meals; he wakened with occasional sour regurgitation into mouth and cough-ing episodes. Antacids helped very briefly; improve-ment noted with OTC histamine receptor blockers. Excellent relief with intensive doses of omeprazole once daily.

Current Symptoms: Above symptoms recurred when medication use stopped after 8 weeks.

Physical Exam: Unremarkable; minimal weight loss.

Clinical Studies: Blood studies: normal. X rays of esophagus and stomach: suggest lower esophagus ulceration. Endoscopy: moderately severe esopha-gitis; longitudinal ridging, denuded mucosa in between. Biopsy: inflamed squamous epithelium.

Diagnosis: Moderately severe gastroesophageal reflux disease without stricture.

Impairment Rating: 14% impairment of the whole person. 16% impairment initially assigned (class 2) based on history, as patient needs continuous medi-cations to remain symptom-free. Adjusted downward to 14% impairment based on absence of weight loss (class 1). No change in grade based on clinical stud-ies (consistent with class 2).

Comment: Persistent untreated gastroesophageal reflux may result in stricture formation, necessitating repeated dilatations and medical therapy resumption. Possible endoscopic luminal procedure or antireflux surgery. Reflux may induce premalignant changes in lower esophagus; regular surveillance and possible surgical treatment increase impairment rating.4,5

EXAMPLE 6-7: DUODENUM DISEASE

Subject: 40-year-old man.

History: 10 years’ intermittent ulcer symptoms. Three bleeding episodes; twice required blood replacement. One transient pyloric obstruction episode.

Current Symptoms: Performance of daily activities repeatedly interrupted. Refuses to consider surgi-cal remedy; requires continuing medical therapy with daily high-dose PPIs to maintain any degree of symptomatic remission. Mild dietary restrictions.

Physical Exam: Height: 1.78 m (5 ft 8 in); weight: 59 kg (130 lb), 7% below desirable.

Clinical Studies: Upper GI tract roentgenograms: marked duodenal bulb cloverleaf deformity with 3-mm ulcer fleck. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy confirms presence of duodenal ulcer with deformity and narrowing of first portion of duodenum. Biopsy specimens taken, negative for H pylori.

Diagnosis: Active duodenal ulcer with a history of recurring complications.

Impairment Rating: 18% impairment of the whole person. History leads to impairment rating of class 2, 16%. Weight loss is consistent with class 2, but objective test results reveal a severe abnormality consistent with class 3, leading to an adjustment upward to 18%.

Comment: Complicated disease; recurrent symp-toms despite medical therapy. H pylori may be fac-tor in chronic complicated duodenal ulcer disease; should be sought and, if found, treated. Other ulcer complications (ie, bleeding) respond to injection or thermal/laser therapy; results equal to surgical treat-ment. Current surgical treatment reserved for ulcers intractable to intensive acid suppression therapy, extremely large duodenal or stomach ulcers, and ulcers associated with malignancy.6

EXAMPLE 6-8: SMALL-INTESTINE DISEASE

Subject: 64-year-old woman.

History: Commercial artist; 5 years’ diarrhea, weight loss, and vague abdominal distress. All symptoms cleared with oral tetracycline and parenteral cyanoco-balamin (vitamin B12). Mild diarrhea for several weeks 2 years ago; subsided with tetracycline.

Current Symptoms: Mild weight loss. No untoward symptoms; mild dietary restrictions, patient tried 1 course of probiotics without relief of symptoms. Patient received monthly intramuscular cyanoco-balamin injections.

Physical Exam: Weight: 49.9 kg (110 lb); pre-illness weight: 54.4 kg (120 lb). Height: 1.55 m (5 ft 1 in).

Clinical Studies: Macrocytic anemia; barium meal examination: extensive small intestine diverticulo-sis. Roentgenographic examination: persistence of numerous diverticula in small intestine, even more

prominent in jejunum. Breath test consistent with small bowel overgrowth.

Diagnosis: Diverticulosis of the small intestine; overgrowth of enteric bacterial flora.

Impairment Rating: 16% impairment due to diver-ticulosis of the small intestine based on history, physical examination findings, and test results; com-bine with appropriate impairment estimate for ane-mia (see Chapter 9, The Hematopoietic System).

Comment: Performs ADLs; unimpaired weight, but patient is dependent on continuing therapy. Diffuse intestinal motility disorder possibly associated with small-intestine diverticulosis may produce a pro-gressively disabling condition, “intestinal pseudo-obstruction,” with abdominal distention, diarrhea, and malnutrition and with little or no response to usual therapy. Possible long-term parenteral feeding; if required, her impairment would advance to class 3 or 4.

EXAMPLE 6-9: PANCREATIC DISEASE OR INJURY

Subject: 35-year-old man.

History: Thrown against steering wheel of truck when it slid off a road. Increasing abdominal pain and distention a few weeks later. Serial ultrasonog-raphy followed by CT scans: expanding pancreatic cyst. No response to bowel rest and parenteral nutrition. Current Symptoms: Intermittent diarrhea, steat-orrhea, and diminished stamina 15 months later that moderately impacts ADLs, despite pancreatic enzyme supplements. Moderate dietary restrictions. Occasional epigastric and back pain.

Physical Exam: Height: 1.9 m (6 ft 3 in); weight: 74.5 kg (164 lb); pre-illness weight: 81.7 kg (180 lb). No evidence of impaired glucose tolerance or diabetes.

Clinical Studies: Blood studies: normal; modest steatorrhea.

Diagnosis: Status after subtotal pancreatectomy con-sequent to trauma, residual chronic pancreatitis and exocrine pancreatic insufficiency.

Impairment Rating: 16% impairment of the whole person (class 2) based on history, weight loss, and objective test results.

Comment: Impaired pancreatic exocrine function; weight maintained within 10% of desirable level. Reduced capacity to perform ADLs.7

CLASS 3 22% to 38% Impairment of the Whole Person

EXAMPLE 6-10: UPPER DIGESTIVE TRACT DISEASE

Subject: 49-year-old man.

History: 5 years’ intermittent retrosternal pain, dys-phagia, and nocturnal regurgitation with occasional and partial remission.

Current Symptoms: Pain less prominent; dyspha-gia more troublesome. Swallows solid foods only with large volumes of liquids. Moderate dietary restrictions.

Physical Exam: Weight: 70.4 kg (155 lb); pre-illness weight: 81.7 kg (180 lb). Height: 1.88 m (6 ft 2 in); lanky and gaunt. Normal vital signs.

Clinical Studies: Chest roentgenogram: mediastinal widening; no lung field densities that might indi-cate aspiration. Barium swallow: markedly dilated and tortuous esophagus terminating in filiform constriction. Esophageal manometry: markedly elevated lower esophageal sphincter pressure without decrease of pressure on swallowing. Endoscopy: no mucosal defect. Successful pneumatic dilation of lower esophageal sphincter after repeated attempts.

Diagnosis: Achalasia of the esophagus.

Impairment Rating: 30% impairment of the whole person based on class 3 history, weight loss, and objective test results.

Comment: Symptoms persistent and progressive despite dietary limitation and esophageal dila-tion; weight loss exceeded 10% of desirable level. Esophagomyotomy highly recommended due to individual’s age, and possible combination of antire-flux procedure. Basic defect in achalasia, and loss of ganglion cells and nerve fibers, cannot be corrected; therapy goal to prevent progressive proximal esopha-geal dilation. Successful treatment could reduce impairment to class 2. Progressive proximal esopha-geal dilation with failure or omission of treatment may result in class 4 rating.4

EXAMPLE 6-11: STOMACH OR DUODENUM DISEASE OR INJURY

Subject: 50-year-old woman.

History: Librarian; partial gastrectomy 2 years ago to remove focus of multiple, dysplastic, adenomatous polyps.

Current Symptoms: Lightheadedness, sweating, and palpitation 15 minutes after meals. Symptoms modified by moderate dietary restriction and lying down. Weight dropped since operation to approxi-mately 15% below desirable.

Physical Exam: Weight: 45.4 kg (100 lb); height: 1.6 m (5 ft 3 in) with a medium frame. Well-healed scar on upper abdomen; physical examination findings otherwise unremarkable.

Clinical Studies: Upper GI tract roentgeno-grams: 70% gastric resection; patent, undistorted gastrojejunostomy.

Diagnosis: Postgastrectomy dumping syndrome.

Impairment Rating: 30% impairment of the whole person based on class 3 history, weight loss, and objective test results.

Comment: Symptoms interfered with performance of normal daily activities despite dietary restriction. Unable to maintain weight within 10% of desirable level.

EXAMPLE 6-12: REGIONAL ENTERITIS

Subject: 38-year-old man.

History: Diarrhea and stamina loss. Partial resec-tion of the distal ileum 3 years ago; evidence of regional enteritis. Several bouts of partial intestinal obstruction, each subsiding with supportive therapy. Required no repeated surgical intervention. Dietary restriction. Oral corticosteroid once a day, oral 5 aminosalicylic acid (5-ASA) therapy daily, vitamin B12: monthly injection and folic acid, oral daily anti-diarrheal agents 4 to 6 times a day. Corticosteroid therapy needed to help sustain adequate health state. Currently receiving anti-tumor necrosis factor (TNF) injections every 6 weeks. Receiving nightly TPN.

Current Symptoms: Episode diarrhea and abdomi-nal cramps.

Physical Exam: Height: 1.6 m (5 ft 3 in); weight: 49.9 kg (110 lb); pre-illness weight: 59 kg (130 lb).

Clinical Studies: Small intestine roentgenogram: segmental distortion consistent with recurrent inflammation and edema.

Diagnosis: Recurrent regional enteritis, with intes-tinal malabsorption and recurring obstruction after ileal resection.

BOTC: An additional 5% impairment is assigned due to daily use of TPN along with 3% due to requirements for daily corticosteroids.

Impairment Rating: 38% impairment of the whole person. History is consistent with class 3, 30%. Physical examination and objective test results are also consistent with class 3, so this impairment per-centage is retained. The BOTC results in the assig-nation of an additional 8% for a total of 38%.

Comment: Only marginal function; impaired nutri-tional state, and weight deficit exceeds 10% of desir-able level despite dietary adjustment and medication. Parenteral nutrition therapy (home treatment pro-gram), administered characteristically at night while person is asleep, greatly reduces degree of impair-ment of many individuals and has maintained nutri-tional status consistent with a class 3 rating, which may improve further to class 2 and permit adjust-ment of the baseline class 3 impairment to 26%. If this is deemed possible, patient may not yet be at MMI. Length and function of remaining normal bowel is an important consideration when assessing severity of impairment.8

EXAMPLE 6-13: PANCREATIC DISEASE

Subject: 45-year-old woman.

History: Chronic abdominal pain secondary to chronic pancreatitis. Reported a 10-year excessive alcohol intake and repeated acute pancreatitis. Diarrhea with steatorrhea over last year helped by pancreatic enzymes. Moderate dietary restrictions

Current Symptoms: Unable to maintain weight; 15% below ideal. Currently abstaining from alcohol.

Physical Exam: Substantial weight loss; abdominal burn marks from heating pads.

Clinical Studies: Abdomen CT scan: calcification throughout pancreas. Endoscopic retrograde cholan-

giopancreatography: normal biliary ductal system. Main pancreatic duct very distorted with abnormal side branches and small 2-mm pseudocyst. No evi-dence of malignancy.

Diagnosis: Chronic pancreatitis with intractable pain; exocrine and endocrine insufficiency.

Impairment Rating: 34% impairment. History and weight loss consistent with class 3, 30%. See Chapter 10, The Endocrine System, for impairment related to diabetes mellitus.

Comment: Impaired exocrine and endocrine pan-creatic functions; continuing treatment necessary. Despite treatment, individual unable to bring weight to within 10% of desirable level. Subtotal pancre-atectomy may be indicated for pain relief attempt. Continuing alcohol use greatly increases mortality.7 Offered surgery for duct and pseudocyst drainage and possible pain management. No surgical benefit for diabetes and malabsorption.

CLASS 4 40% to 60% Impairment of the Whole Person

EXAMPLE 6-14: UPPER DIGESTIVE TRACT DISEASE

Subject: 62-year-old man.

History: Total gastrectomy 3 years ago for treatment of stomach cancer. Esophagoenterostomy (Hunt-Lawrence pouch) constructed. Oral vitamins.

Current Symptoms: Postoperative anorexia and early satiety; unrelenting weight loss and signs of nutritional deficiency. Marked fatigue, weakness, and inability to read or write except for brief periods. Severe dietary restrictions.

Physical Exam: Height: 1.75 m (5 ft 9 in); weight: 52.7 kg (116 lb). Malnourished; appears older than stated age. Tongue smooth and glistening. No pal-pated masses in vicinity of healed upper abdominal scar. Slight pedal edema.

Diagnosis: Postoperative absence of the stomach with esophagojejunal anastomosis; secondary nutri-tional deficiency.

Impairment Rating: 60%. 50% impairment based on history. Weight loss also consistent with class 4 impairment, as is total gastrectomy, warranting use of highest rating for class (60%). This is combined with appropriate anemia impairment estimate (see Chapter 9, The Hematopoietic System) to determine whole person impairment.

Comment: Weight loss exceeds 20% of desirable level; evidence of marked nutritional deficiency. Individual unable to perform many ADLs. If he con-tinues to be free of recurrent cancer, consider supple-mental parenteral nutrition therapy (home treatment program).

EXAMPLE 6-15: UPPER DIGESTIVE TRACT DISEASE

Subject: 58-year-old man.

History: Almost complete esophageal obstruction. Extensive lower esophagus and proximal stomach resection due to cancer 5 years ago. No evidence of tumor recurrence by CT imaging and endoscopic studies. Early satiety severely restricts eating ability; primarily able to take only liquids.

Current Symptoms: Gastrostomy tube for feeding. Dilation of strictured esophagus required once a month to accommodate saliva secretion.

Physical Exam: Height: 1.78 m (5 ft 10 in); weight: 49.9 kg (110 lb); pre-illness weight: 68.1 kg (150 lb).

EXAMPLE 6-16: PANCREATIC DISEASE

Subject: 47-year-old man.

History: Manufacturer’s representative; 13 months prior onset of vague abdominal pain, weight loss, and uncharacteristic depression, followed by gradu-ally deepening jaundice. 6.4 Enterocutaneous Fistulas

Evaluate permanent enterocutaneous fistulas of the GI tract, biliary tract, or pancreas that are associ-ated with diseases of these structures or their treat-ment as part of the primarily involved organ system. Permanent, surgically created stomas usually are provided to compensate for anatomic losses and to allow either ingress to or egress from the alimentary tract. There is no additional impairment given to individuals who use these for nutrition, as the BOTC is included in the rating for the ostomy. However, the higher rating should be used for these individuals. Likewise, the highest rating for each category should be used if the history or examination indicates that the stoma is not functioning optimally or interferes significantly with ADLs. These ratings are carried forward from the Fifth Edition.

If an individual has a permanent, surgically cre-ated stoma, combine a percentage based on Table 6-7 with an estimate based on criteria related to the involved organ (see the Combined Values Chart in the Appendix). 6.5 Liver and Biliary Tract

6.5a Criteria for Rating Permanent Impairment due to Liver or Biliary Tract Disease

Impairment due to liver disease or injury may be due to traumatic injury, exposure to viral or parasitic agents, or toxic exposure. Such impairments are rated from this section and Table 6-8.

Significant gallbladder disease usually results in cho-lecystectomy, which usually results in no significant symptoms or problems (0% impairment). Following

Subject: 30-year-old man.

History: Occupational exposure to methylene chloride. Presented to his primary care physician with complaints of malaise. Liver enzyme elevation present, but resolved completely after removal from occupational exposure.

Current Symptoms: None.

Physical Exam: Normal.

Clinical Studies: Liver enzymye levels (aspartate aminotransferase [AST], alanine aminotransferase [ALT]) bilirubin levels, and prothrombin time are all normal.

Class 3: 30% to 42% impairment due to liver disease and 21% to 29% from biliary tract disease.

Subject: 46-year-old woman.

Ingested no drugs known to cause cholestasis; antimitochondrial anti-body test positive. Using cyproheptadine hydrochlo-ride (Periactin) and diphenhydramine hydrochloride (Benadryl) 4 or more times a day for pruritus.

Current Symptoms: Recent significantly increased impairment: unable to complete all daily activities due to increasing debility.

Comment: Primary biliary cirrhosis is a relent-lessly progressive liver disease that leads to class 4 impairment. Currently, most recipients report a remark-able improvement in quality of life and many enjoy normal lifestyles, although compliance with drug therapies and follow-up visits are required. Subject: 55-year-old woman.

History: Repeated acute cholecystitis attacks for 5 years. Refused to seek medical care because of reli-gious beliefs.

Current Symptoms: Increasingly frequent and severe bouts of right upper quadrant pain, nausea, vomiting, fever, jaundice, dark urine, and pruritus. Unable to perform many basic ADLs for more than a year and is intermittently confused.

Physical Exam: Jaundiced and cachectic, with right upper quadrant pain to palpitation. Oriented inter-mittently to place and location.

Clinical Studies: Laboratory tests: biliary obstruc-tion and advanced liver damage. Ultrasound reveals calculi in gallbladder and common bile duct. Liver biopsy specimen: advanced biliary cirrhosis. Declined any consideration of an invasive procedure that might alleviate disease.

Diagnosis: Biliary cirrhosis, secondary to recurrent and progressive obstruction of bile ducts.

Impairment Rating: 75% impairment of the whole person based on liver and biliary tract disease. Her biliary tract disease meets all 3 criteria for class 3 disease. Her liver disease is class 4 throughout. Combining the maximum impairment grades for each (29% combined with 65%) leads to an impair-ment rating of 75%.

Comment: Severe and irreparable impairment of liver and biliary tract function. Needs live-in assistance to perform normal ADLs. Laparoscopic removal of calculus-containing gallbladder, endo-scopic extraction of common bile duct stones, and variety of radiologic, endoscopic, and surgical bili-ary drainage procedures may greatly reduce the total impairment rating.13

6.6 Hernias

6.6a Criteria for Rating Permanent Impairment due to Herniation

Criteria for evaluating impairment due to abdomi-nal herniation are listed in Table 6-10. A typical successful hernia repair will usually result in a 0% impairment rating. If there are pain com-plaints due to residual nerve entrapment, please see the CNS chapter (Chapter 13). Diaphragmatic hernias are rated at 2% whole person impairment if successfully repaired or at 5% whole person impairment if unrepaired and asymptomatic. If they affect digestive function, Section 6.2, Upper Digestive Tract, is used to rate the impairment. If the diaphragmatic hernias affect respiration, the criteria for restrictive lung disease are used to rate the impairment. Physical findings are the key factor.
